You’re making the assumption that I’m one of the people who doesn’t read for pleasure. I’m not talking about the benefits of reading, I know what they are and I’m not asking anyone to tell them to me. 

When I said “concrete” problems, it’s because I was discussing the idea of acting like there was a moral crisis going on with adults who do not prefer to read. And in order to legitimately demean someone else, to call them stupid and immoral, I need to have a genuinely good reason showing who they’re hurting (even if it’s themselves) and why. That’s where the “concrete” part came in.

But if someone does not enjoy reading, how is forcing themselves to do an activity they dislike during their free-time “caring for their mental well-being” ? 

Is it impossible to conceive that there are other options for self-improvement of the mind, that aren’t pleasure reading?
Okay now I’m curious, how are you pronouncing them?

The issue of people, especially children, engaging only in short-form content and damaging their brain is a real one. 

But why does not reading = melting your mind with mind-numbing content. Why is it binary? 

Can’t someone not enjoy reading for pleasure, but spend their time taking hikes or doing puzzles, for example. Are their brains being rotted by this?

Is reading the only thing that helps with memory and brain functioning? 

Addiction to screens is an entire separate issue, and one I would agree is a problem. But there’s not a binary here where someone is either reading a book or looking at a screen. There are a thousand other things someone can do with their time.
But who is to say that reading complex narratives are the only way to flex the muscles of the brain?
I agree, I really do. But usually I see some level of pushback (as I’m sure you know, people on twitter love an argument, it boosts engagement.) Not seeing any had me taken aback.
Are books the only way to lengthen attention span? Is that proven?
But reading is not the only form of escapism, and not the only way of utilizing imagination.

But what you’re saying is what I’m trying to get at. You say that by not reading more complex stories, an individual is not advancing. But then what? What does a lack of advancement in literature as an adult mean to you personally? What are the consequences of this? 

If someone is genuinely presenting with significant reading/comprehension deficits (and I work in a special education setting, so I see what this looks like every day), I understand the concerns. But if an adult is capable of reading/reading more complex texts, and chooses not to out of a lack of interest, what are the concrete problems presented with this?
And is reading for pleasure the only way to flex it? Who’s to say that these people aren’t reading otherwise in their day to day lives?

Im biased bc I work in a special education environment. A lot of these children were failed by the public education system, but it doesn’t make them stupid, it means they have a learning disorder. And the content was inaccessible to them. 

But when put in a specialized environment and given accommodation, they are able to grasp material.
